name: Great Zimbabwe
summary: A Shona kingdom on the Zimbabwean plateau, rich from cattle and the gold trade to the Indian Ocean. Its capital, Great Zimbabwe, is the largest stone structure in precolonial southern Africa.

knownFor.label: Zimbabwe birds
knownFor.note: Carved soapstone birds, now the national emblem.

knownFor.label: Gold trade
knownFor.note: Gold traded to the Swahili coast.

location.value: The Zimbabwean plateau in southern Africa (modern Zimbabwe), with its capital at Great Zimbabwe.
location.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

terrain.value: A granite plateau between the Zambezi and Limpopo rivers, with goldfields.
terrain.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

resources.value: Gold, cattle, and farmland for sorghum and millet.
resources.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

disasters.value: Shona oral tradition blames the city’s end on a “salt shortage”, possibly meaning exhausted land and resources.
disasters.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

population.value: The capital had perhaps 10,000 people at its peak. Older estimates said up to 18,000–20,000.
population.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

urbanisation.value: Great Zimbabwe covered 7.22 km² at its height, and over 150 smaller “zimbabwes” were spread across the kingdom.
urbanisation.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

disease.value: Not documented in the sources checked.

migration.value: Around 1450, Nyatsimba Mutota led people north to found the Mutapa Empire.
migration.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

economicBase.value: Cattle, agriculture, and control of gold trade routes.
economicBase.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

tradeRoutes.value: Gold and ivory were exported via Swahili city-states (Sofala, Kilwa) into the Indian Ocean trade. Persian and Chinese ceramics have been found at the site.
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible; finds include Chinese pottery and Persian glass.

moneyAndTax.value: No coinage. The kingdom taxed tributary rulers.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

inequality.value: An increasingly rigid three-tier class structure: royalty in the Great Enclosure and Hill Complex, nobles, and commoners outside.
inequality.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

governmentType.value: A monarchy under a sacred king (mambo), supported by spirit mediums.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026) (infobox)

keyRulers.value: Few names are known. One historian (Ken Mufuka) names Chigwagu Rusvingo as the first mambo.
keyRulers.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

succession.value: Royal succession. The details are unknown.

institutions.value: The mambo was assisted by a designated sibling. Tributary rulers had their own “zimbabwes”.
institutions.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

stability.value: Not well documented; the city was used for about 200–300 years.

armyAndTech.value: Not well documented. The great walls were probably more about prestige than defence.

majorWars.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026) (infobox)

alliancesRivals.value: Replaced Mapungubwe as the main power. Was later replaced by Mutapa and Butua (Khami).
alliancesRivals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

inventions.value: Dry-stone masonry without mortar, in coursed, chequered and herringbone patterns, at its height in the 13th–15th centuries. Iron smelting.
inventions.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

scienceEducation.value: Oral knowledge. The Great Enclosure may have hosted initiation schools (domba).
scienceEducation.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

openness.value: Connected to the wider Indian Ocean world through trade.
openness.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

communicationTransport.value: Travel on foot; trade routes to the Swahili coast at Sofala.

religion.value: Shona traditional religion, with spirit mediums (svikiro) and ancestor veneration. The Zimbabwe Birds (soapstone carvings) may be sacred symbols.
religion.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

artsArchitecture.value: The Great Enclosure (13th–14th centuries), the largest ancient stone structure south of the Sahara, plus soapstone bird carvings.
artsArchitecture.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

socialStructure.value: Royalty, nobles, commoners. Metalworking was men’s work.
socialStructure.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

sharedIdentity.value: A Shona heritage. Modern Zimbabwe is named after the site, and the Zimbabwe Bird is on its flag.
sharedIdentity.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

dailyLife.value: Round daga (clay) houses with thatched roofs, within stone enclosures for the elite; sorghum, millet and cattle.

neighbours.value: Mapungubwe, the Swahili coast cities, and later Mutapa and Butua.
neighbours.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

ideasReligions.value: Indian Ocean trade connected it to Arabia, Persia, India and China.
ideasReligions.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

colonisation.value: Not a coloniser. Colonial-era writers falsely denied its African origin; African construction only became the accepted consensus by the 1950s.
colonisation.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

riseSignals.value: Control of the gold trade as routes shifted north from Mapungubwe (by 1250–1300), plus cattle wealth.
riseSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

peakPeriod.value: The 14th century, when the Great Enclosure was built.
peakPeriod.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

declineSignals.value: Exhausted land and resources, reduced gold demand in the early 15th century, and trade shifting to the Zambezi route. The cause is not known for certain.
declineSignals.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

outcome.value: Replacement. By the 16th century, Mutapa and Butua (Khami) had replaced it. The site was abandoned by the 16th–17th century.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Archaeology, Portuguese accounts (from the 16th century), and Shona oral tradition. Checked against Wikipedia on 6 Nov 2026. See also Pikirayi (2001).
sources.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)

overallCertainty.value: Low to moderate. There are no written sources from the time. Rulers, population and the causes of decline are uncertain.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Kingdom of Great Zimbabwe (checked 6 Nov 2026)
